gist: When the question asks for the highest / lowest / most / least / top N / 2nd-highest entity, gold ranks the joined rows once with ORDER BY <metric> DESC|ASC LIMIT N on the OUTERMOST query. A query that has no ordering at all, or hides the ranking in a subquery and matches the outer rows by equality (WHERE metric = (SELECT ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1)), returns ties, duplicates, or the wrong row set.
bad_pattern: The question contains a superlative cue (highest, lowest, most, least, largest, smallest, oldest, youngest, best, worst, top N, 2nd/3rd highest, maximum, minimum) about an ENTITY or its attribute, and the outermost SELECT has neither ORDER BY ... LIMIT N nor a bare MAX/MIN aggregate in its own SELECT list. Two shapes: (a) no ranking anywhere: SELECT s.f_name, s.l_name ... WHERE c.name = 'Advanced Database Systems' with no ORDER BY, for 'Name the students ... with the highest satisfaction'; (b) ranking pushed into a subquery and re-joined by equality: WHERE r.sat = (SELECT r2.sat ... ORDER BY r2.sat DESC LIMIT 1), or WHERE e.event_id IN (SELECT event_id FROM events ORDER BY timestamp ASC LIMIT 2) for 'the top 2 oldest events', or WHERE a."PREVALENCE RATE" = (SELECT "PREVALENCE RATE" ... ORDER BY ... DESC LIMIT 1) for 'patients with the most prevalent conditions'. Gold for all three: the same joins, then ORDER BY <metric> DESC|ASC LIMIT N on the outer query and no subquery. Concrete pairs (BIRD train): BAD `SELECT s.f_name, s.l_name FROM student AS s JOIN registration AS r ON s.student_id = r.student_id JOIN course AS c ON r.course_id = c.course_id WHERE c.name = 'Advanced Database Systems' AND r.sat = (SELECT r2.sat FROM registration AS r2 JOIN course AS c2 ON r2.course_id = c2.course_id WHERE c2.name = 'Advanced Database Systems' ORDER BY r2.sat DESC LIMIT 1)` -> GOOD `SELECT s.f_name, s.l_name FROM student AS s INNER JOIN registration AS r ON s.student_id = r.student_id INNER JOIN course AS c ON r.course_id = c.course_id WHERE c.name = 'Advanced Database Systems' ORDER BY r.sat DESC LIMIT 1` ('students ... with the highest satisfaction'); BAD `SELECT DISTINCT lc.category FROM events e JOIN ... WHERE e.event_id IN (SELECT event_id FROM events ORDER BY timestamp ASC LIMIT 2)` -> GOOD `SELECT T4.category FROM events_relevant AS T1 INNER JOIN app_events_relevant AS T2 ON T1.event_id = T2.event_id INNER JOIN app_labels AS T3 ON T3.app_id = T2.app_id INNER JOIN label_categories AS T4 ON T3.label_id = T4.label_id ORDER BY T1.timestamp LIMIT 2` ('categories of the top 2 oldest events').
correct_pattern: Same FROM/JOIN/WHERE as the candidate minus the ranking subquery, plus ORDER BY <metric column> DESC (highest/most/largest/latest) or ASC (lowest/least/smallest/oldest) LIMIT N on the outermost query, where N is the number the question names (default 1; '2nd-highest' is LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1). The entity columns are selected directly from the joined rows. A superlative that refers to a COUNT per group ('the country with the most stations') becomes GROUP BY <entity> ORDER BY COUNT(...) DESC LIMIT 1.
fix: CHECK FIRST: (i) does the hint map the superlative word to a literal filter (e.g. 'highest score' refers to rating_score = 5)? If yes, return unchanged. (ii) Does the question ask only for the maximum VALUE (a number) and the SQL returns MAX(metric)? If yes, return unchanged. (iii) Does the outermost query already have ORDER BY <metric> ... LIMIT N? If yes, return unchanged. (iv) Is the outermost SELECT a single aggregate (COUNT, SUM or AVG) without GROUP BY, so that the answer is a number computed over the rows of the top entity (e.g. 'how many shipments were delivered by the oldest truck')? If yes, the ranking must stay where it is: return unchanged. Only when none of (i)-(iv) holds: Remove the equality-against-ranking-subquery (or add the missing ordering) and append ORDER BY <metric> DESC|ASC LIMIT N to the outermost query, selecting the same entity columns. SCOPE WARNING: this rule is ONLY about where the ranking lives. Do not add DISTINCT; if the outermost SELECT is a SELECT DISTINCT and you add ORDER BY ... LIMIT N, remove that DISTINCT (with LIMIT it can return an arbitrary row), do not change which columns are selected, do not add IS NOT NULL guards, do not change join types or unrelated WHERE conditions. If the superlative word describes a filter value the hint already maps to a literal (e.g. 'fastest delivery' -> Ship Mode = 'First Class', 'highest score' -> rating_score = 5), there is nothing to rank and this rule does NOT apply. If the question asks only for the maximum VALUE (a number, not an entity), MAX(metric) is fine and this rule does NOT apply. DECLINE: if after these checks you judge that this rule does not fit the question, return the SQL unchanged and leave applied_rules empty; that is a correct answer, not a failure.

gist: BIRD gold is almost always one SELECT over joined tables, at most one subquery. A candidate with a WITH clause, or three or more query levels, when the question gives no reason for it (no 'among those who', no 'more than the average', no 'at least one', no comparison between two groups computed separately) is usually answering a different, more elaborate question and gets the numbers wrong on the way. On the train slice 12 of 13 such top answers were wrong.
bad_pattern: The question is a plain count / list / percentage / lookup, and the SQL uses a CTE (WITH ...) or stacks derived tables, FROM (SELECT ...) AS a, (SELECT ...) AS b, (SELECT ...) AS c, or a UNION ALL of several tables inside FROM, or a LEFT JOIN against a CTE to test existence. Real failures: 'Find the difference in percentage of the movies under keywords A and B' -> three derived tables (count A, count B, total) divided in the outer SELECT (gold: ONE pass with SUM(CASE WHEN keyword_name = A THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) - SUM(CASE WHEN ... = B ...) over keyword JOIN movie_keywords); 'What percentage of women do not have applications installed ... with respect to men?' -> WITH installed_devices AS (SELECT DISTINCT device_id ...) then LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL (gold: gender_age JOIN events JOIN app_events WHERE is_installed = 0, SUM(CASE gender='F') / SUM(CASE gender='M')); 'How many orders with quantity > 5 shipped by First Class?' -> COUNT(*) over a UNION ALL of central/east/south/west_superstore (gold: one regional table, no UNION); 'product name with the highest quantity in a single purchase' -> UNION ALL of four regional tables then ORDER BY (gold: east_superstore JOIN product WHERE Region = 'East' ORDER BY Quantity DESC LIMIT 1). Concrete pair (BIRD train, 'Find the difference in percentage of the movies under keywords of "woman director" and "independent film"'): BAD `SELECT ((CAST(w.cnt AS REAL) - CAST(i.cnt AS REAL)) * 100.0 / t.total) FROM (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT mk.movie_id) AS cnt FROM movie_keywords mk JOIN keyword k ON mk.keyword_id = k.keyword_id WHERE k.keyword_name = 'woman director') w, (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT mk.movie_id) AS cnt ... WHERE k.keyword_name = 'independent film') i, (SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM movie) t` -> GOOD `SELECT CAST((SUM(CASE WHEN T1.keyword_name = 'woman director' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) - SUM(CASE WHEN T1.keyword_name = 'independent film' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)) AS REAL) * 100 / SUM(CASE WHEN T1.keyword_name = 'independent film' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM keyword AS T1 INNER JOIN movie_keywords AS T2 ON T1.keyword_id = T2.keyword_id`.
correct_pattern: One SELECT over the needed tables joined on their keys, filters in WHERE, conditional sums written as SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) or SUM(cond) in the same SELECT, percentages as CAST(SUM(...) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(...) over the SAME rows, existence as a JOIN + WHERE on the flag column rather than a CTE with LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL. When several same-shaped tables exist (regional copies), gold queries ONE of them, not a UNION ALL; pick the one the question or hint names, otherwise leave the query unchanged (do not guess a region). A single subquery is allowed when the question itself needs a second aggregate (e.g. 'above the average', 'the total of all movies'); then this rule does NOT apply.
fix: CHECK FIRST: (i) does the question contain 'among those', 'who also', 'more than the average', 'at least one', 'each ... that has', or compare two separately computed groups? If yes, return unchanged. (ii) Does the question itself need a second aggregate (above the average, the total of all ...)? If yes, one subquery is expected: return unchanged. (iii) Is the nesting a UNION ALL of same-shaped tables and neither question nor hint names one of them? If yes, return unchanged. Only when none of (i)-(iii) holds: Rewrite as one flat SELECT with the same tables, keys and literal filters, moving each per-branch count into a SUM(CASE ...) term in the outer SELECT and each existence test into a JOIN + WHERE. SCOPE WARNING: keep the literals, the join keys, the selected columns and the arithmetic of the candidate; the ONLY change is removing the nesting. Do not add DISTINCT, do not change the output columns, do not introduce ORDER BY or LIMIT, do not change which tables are read except to drop a UNION ALL of same-shaped tables when the question names one of them. If the question text contains 'among those', 'who also', 'more than the average', 'at least one', 'each ... that has', or compares two separately computed groups, the nesting is justified and this rule does NOT apply. DECLINE: if after these checks you judge that this rule does not fit the question, return the SQL unchanged and leave applied_rules empty; that is a correct answer, not a failure.
